item.title: One mouse neuron, 70 cm of wiring: the brain's alertness system mapped
item.description: Allen Institute researchers mapped the locus coeruleus, the tiny brainstem 'blue spot' that makes noradrenaline (alertness, attention, stress), in mice. They imaged nearly 35,000 of its neurons across the whole brain and fully reconstructed dozens of them: the average axon is about 35 cm long, and one reached 70.32 cm of total branched length inside a mouse brain about 1 cm long. item.title: A Robot Knee-Jerk Reflex With No Sensor or Chip
item.description: Tohoku University engineers built a reflex for robot muscles out of air, a mechanical valve and a string. When an artificial muscle is stretched past a set length, a parallel "spindle" muscle pulls a string that opens the valve, and the muscle contracts. No electronic sensor or chip is involved. item.title: Fear makes your brain blur danger and safety
item.description: McGill researchers put mice in an augmented-reality arena that could switch instantly between a 'danger' and a 'safety' context, while miniature microscopes recorded hundreds of neurons in the ventral hippocampus. item.title: Webb found a star with no fusion inside
item.description: JWST spotted MoM-BH*-1 at cosmic dawn, a few hundred million years after the Big Bang. It looks like a star but puts out ~100 billion times more energy than any star could. The team's best explanation is a black hole of ~100,000 solar masses wrapped in a dense gas cocoon about the size of our solar system: a 'black hole star', where the light comes from accretion, not fusion. item.title: The "Lonely" Sleep Waves of the Aging Brain
item.description: During deep sleep, large groups of neurons go quiet and switch back on together, and these slow waves travel across the brain from front to back. A UC Berkeley team compared overnight EEG in 61 young and 75 older adults. item.title: A Neural Network That Computes With Light in a Fiber
item.description: Researchers at the University of Tokyo and NTT built a neural network around a single loop of optical fiber. Light pulses circling the loop do the computing. Their new training method, state-skipping direct feedback alignment, learns from the final error and never needs to read the loop's hidden states. item.title: How an Octopus Pours Itself Through a Tiny Hole
item.description: How does a soft animal with eight arms get its whole body through a hole narrower than the gap between its eyes? Researchers filmed three common octopuses crossing a clear partition 30 times. Every pass followed the same order: probe with one arm, push 3–5 arms through, then anchor and pull.
